title: Feature Stores
summary: The infrastructure piece that keeps training and serving features consistent, and prevents the subtle bugs that arise when they don't.

slides.subTitle: Training/serving skew
slides.markdown: A model is trained on features computed by one pipeline (often batch SQL or a data-science notebook, working over historical data) but served in production by a **different** pipeline (often a low-latency service computing features on the fly from live data). If those two pipelines compute the "same" feature even slightly differently — different rounding, a different time window, a null handled differently — the model sees systematically different inputs at serving time than it learned from, silently degrading accuracy with no code error anywhere. This mismatch is called **training-serving skew**, and it's one of the most common, hardest-to-detect bugs in production ML. A feature store's core purpose is eliminating this by making both training and serving pull from **one shared feature definition**.

slides.subTitle: Fed from the same feature definitions
slides.markdown:
A feature store typically splits into two physical stores sharing one logical definition. The **offline store** holds historical feature values (often in a data warehouse), optimized for scanning large volumes to build training datasets. The **online store** holds the latest feature values (often in a low-latency key-value store like Redis), optimized for fetching a single entity's features in milliseconds during serving. Both are populated by the same feature computation logic, defined once — this is the structural guarantee against skew, since there's no second, independently-written implementation to drift out of sync.

slides.subTitle: Avoiding future leakage
slides.markdown: When building a training dataset by joining historical feature values to historical labels, you must join each label to the feature values **as they existed at that label's timestamp** — not the feature's current (or future) value. Get this wrong and you get **future leakage**: e.g. training a churn model using a customer's "total lifetime purchases" feature computed with today's full total, when at the actual historical prediction time the customer hadn't made those later purchases yet — the model learns from information it wouldn't have had in production, producing offline metrics that look great but collapse in production. Feature stores implement **point-in-time joins** specifically to get this right automatically, since doing it manually and correctly at scale is notoriously error-prone.

slides.subTitle: Across teams and models
slides.markdown: Feature stores let a feature be defined **once** ("7-day rolling average order value") and reused across many models and teams, instead of each team reimplementing similar logic slightly differently — which is itself a common source of subtle bugs and duplicated engineering effort. **Versioning** matters because feature definitions evolve (a bug fix, a new time window): a model in production needs to keep using the exact feature version it was trained on until it's deliberately retrained against a new version, otherwise you get an unplanned, undocumented change in a live model's inputs. This combination — shared definitions plus explicit versioning — is what lets an organization scale feature engineering across many models without either duplicated work or silent breakage.

slides.subTitle: Same feature, computed differently, twice
slides.markdown: Without a feature store, it's easy to end up with a **training** implementation of a feature (say, Python/pandas in a notebook, computing "days since last login") and a completely separate **serving** implementation (say, Java in a production service, computing the same concept) — written by different people, at different times, with subtly different edge-case handling (timezone handling, how "never logged in" is treated). Both look correct in isolation; the mismatch only shows up as an unexplained accuracy gap between offline evaluation and production performance, which is exactly why training-serving skew is so hard to debug after the fact — nothing throws an error, the two implementations just quietly disagree on some inputs.

slides.sectionTitle: Lightweight feature table vs full platform
slides.subTitle: When the overhead is worth it
slides.markdown:
| | Lightweight feature table (shared SQL view/table) | Full feature-store platform (Feast, Tecton) |
|---|---|---|
| Setup cost | Low — a well-organized shared table or view | Higher — new infrastructure, new team skill |
| Solves skew | Partially, if both training and serving genuinely read the same table | Fully, with built-in online/offline consistency guarantees |
| Point-in-time joins | Manual, error-prone at scale | Built-in |
| Fits | A handful of models, one team, low serving-latency needs | Many models across teams, strict low-latency serving, frequent feature reuse |

How to decide: start with a well-governed shared table — it solves most of the skew problem cheaply for a small setup. Move to a full feature-store platform once you have enough models/teams that manual point-in-time correctness and cross-team feature governance become a real, recurring cost.
